items.title: What ?? and || do with an empty string
items.body:
The key is right: `'' ?? 'fallback'` is `''`, and `'' || 'fallback'` is `'fallback'`. The two operators answer different questions. `??` (nullish coalescing) falls back only when the left side is `null` or `undefined`. An empty string is neither, so it is kept. `||` falls back for any **falsy** value: `false`, `0`, `''`, `null`, `undefined` and `NaN`. An empty string is falsy, so it is replaced. That is why D1's hypothesis is false, and the lab says the repair is the explanation, not a rewrite of the algorithm.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Both keep the empty string": `||` does not.
- "?? is the stricter one about empties": it is the reverse; `??` keeps empties.
- "Both treat '' as missing": only `||` does.

excerpts.quote: Nullish coalescing falls back only for `null` or `undefined`. It preserves the empty string. Logical OR falls back for every falsy value, including the empty string.
The repair here is the explanation, not an unnecessary algorithm rewrite.

items.title: Why "PASS 3439" alone proves nothing
items.body:
The key is right: without the command you cannot tell whose code ran, and the default run grades the reference solutions. In `verify.cjs`, `const mode = starters ? 'starter' : 'solution'`: unless you pass `--starters`, it loads the files in `solutions/`. Both runs print the same kind of `PASS 3439` line. So a note with just that line might mean "my code passed" or "the reference answer passed", and a reviewer cannot tell which. The chapter's rule: write the exact command beside every result.

Why the others are wrong:
- "PASS lines are cached": the verifier runs the tests each time; nothing is cached.
- "3439 is a warm-up everyone passes": the issue is ambiguity, not difficulty.
- "The verifier never prints PASS": it does print `'PASS ' + r.id` for each passing capstone, as well as writing JSON.

excerpts.quote: const mode=starters?'starter':'solution',results=[];
console.log('PASS '+r.id);
Write the exact command beside every result. "PASS 3439" alone cannot tell a reviewer whose implementation ran.

items.title: Why keeping base in a conflict is the wrong repair
items.body:
The key is right: it silently rewrites the published local-wins policy that the contract states. The prompt is explicit: when both sides changed differently, "record a conflict and keep local (including local deletion)". Returning base instead may *feel* safer, because it brings deleted text back, but it is a different product decision made inside the code. The lab says product policy belongs in the contract, and code should not improvise a different policy during an exceptional-looking case. The existing test with a locally deleted key and a remote edit is there to catch exactly this.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Base may be missing, so it can throw": the reader returns a sentinel for absence; nothing throws.
- "Leaves conflicts unsorted": which value is kept does not change the order in which keys are visited.
- "Slower, a third lookup": all three values are already read for every key.

excerpts.quote: otherwise record a conflict and keep local (including local deletion).

Explain why keeping base violates the published local-wins policy, even if the restored text feels safer. Product policy belongs in the contract; code should not improvise a different policy during an exceptional-looking case.

items.title: What happens when all three versions of a key differ
items.body:
The key is right: the key is recorded in `conflicts` and local's state wins, even if local deleted it. Walk the rule in order. Local does not equal remote. Local does not equal base, so remote is not "the only change". Remote does not equal base either, so local is not "the only change". Both sides moved differently, so the last clause fires: `conflicts.push(key)` and `selected = localValue`. If local had deleted the key, `localValue` is the missing sentinel, and the key is left out of `value` while its name stays in `conflicts`.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Remote wins as newer": the contract never looks at time and names local as the winner.
- "Dropped from both until a human decides": the key is listed in conflicts, and local's state is used.
- "Base is restored": the contract keeps local, not base.

excerpts.quote: } else { conflicts.push(key); selected = localValue;
A conflicted local deletion therefore removes the key while retaining its name in `conflicts`.

items.title: How conflicts come out sorted without being sorted
items.body:
The key is right: the union of keys is sorted once and visited in order, so conflict names arrive already sorted. The loop is `for (const key of [...allKeys].sort())`. Every key, conflicting or not, is processed in alphabetical order, and `conflicts.push(key)` appends names in that same order. So the array is sorted the moment the loop ends. The worked trace notes the cost: sorting k keys is O(k log k), once.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Object.fromEntries sorts": it only builds the `value` object; `conflicts` is a separate array.
- "conflicts is a Set": it is a plain array; and Sets keep insertion order, not sorted order.
- "The verifier sorts before comparing": the contract requires sorted output, and the reference achieves it itself.

excerpts.quote: for (const key of [...allKeys].sort()) {
Keys are visited in sorted order, so `conflicts` is lexicographically sorted // without a second sort.
The union of own keys is sorted once, so conflicts are lexicographic.

items.title: Start here: the advanced practice route and capstone 3439
items.body:
This repo is a collection of JavaScript exercises. The `advanced-practice/` folder is a six-chapter route that turns them into **evidence**: can you reason about a contract, reproduce a failure, and explain it? Every quiz in this pack centres on one capstone, **3439**, a three-way merge of flat records, plus the verifier that grades capstones.

Suggested reading order (the route's own README lists it):

1. `advanced-practice/README.md`.
2. `01-placement-and-route.md`, especially "Understand the verifier before trusting it".
3. `02-worked-merge-trace.md`: one merge traced key by key, then three boundary topics.
4. `03-debugging-laboratory.md`: four labs (D1 to D4) that reject plausible but false explanations.
5. `04-independent-exercises.md`, then `05-solutions-and-review.md` only after recording an attempt.

Keep three files open: the prompt `js-capstones/prompts/3439.txt` (the contract, one paragraph), the reference `js-capstones/solutions/3439.cjs` (58 lines with a long comment), and `js-capstones/verify.cjs`.

excerpts.quote: This six-chapter route turns the existing exercises into evidence that you can reason about contracts, reproduce failures, and transfer a technique to a new problem.
The authoritative local contract is [prompt 3439](../js-capstones/prompts/3439.txt), with examples in [its tests](../js-capstones/tests/3439.cjs).

items.title: Why plain record[key] misreads a side
items.body:
The key is right: an inherited property of that name reads as present, although the side does not own the key. `record[key]` returns whatever value is **visible**, and that includes values inherited from the object's prototype chain. If one side owns a key and another side merely inherits a property with the same name, plain lookup makes the second side look as if it has a value, so the merge compares the wrong thing. The reference's `read` helper uses `Object.hasOwn(record, key)` and returns the missing sentinel otherwise. The lab's heading puts it in four words: ownership is not lookup.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Numeric keys collide": object keys are strings; this lab is about inheritance.
- "undefined own values disappear": lookup returns an own `undefined` fine; values are strings here anyway.
- "Getters run twice": accessors are outside this exercise's domain (D4).

excerpts.quote: Now show why a reader that merely performs `record[key]` can misclassify the other side.
const read = (record, key) => (Object.hasOwn(record, key) ? record[key] : missing);
A lookup without `Object.hasOwn` also reads inherited values

items.title: What a three-way merge is
items.body:
Two people edit copies of the same document. To combine their work you need three versions: **base** (the common starting point), **local** (your edit) and **remote** (theirs). Comparing each side with base tells you who changed what. If only one side changed a key, take that side's change. If both made the same change, there is nothing to decide.

Capstone 3439 applies this per key to flat records of string values, and adds two twists to watch for:

- **Deletion is absence.** A side that deleted a key simply does not have it. The merge needs a way to compare "missing" like any other value.
- **Order and shape of the answer.** The result is exactly `{value, conflicts}`, the inputs must not change, and the prompt has a requirement about the order of `conflicts`.

Read the prompt's rule sentence slowly; the order of its "otherwise" clauses is the algorithm. Then follow the worked trace's table, one row per key, before reading the reference code.

excerpts.quote: Three flat records contain own enumerable string values. The function returns exactly `{value, conflicts}` and does not mutate inputs. Deletion is represented by an absent own property.
otherwise whichever side still matches base is the one that did not change,

items.title: Evidence habits: commands, hypotheses, one change at a time
items.body:
The route cares less about passing tests than about what your evidence actually proves. Three habits run through it:

- **Record the command.** Read `verify.cjs` and chapter 1's section on the verifier: list its flags, what each one makes it grade or print, and what it does by default. Then ask what a result written down without its command would really tell a reader.
- **Reject hypotheses with direct observation.** The debugging lab starts each case from a persuasive explanation and asks you to test it with the smallest possible input before changing any code. Sometimes the right repair is to the explanation, not the algorithm.
- **One mutation at a time.** When you break a copy of the code on purpose, change one thing, so that a failing test points at one cause.

The lab ends with an incident note another learner could reproduce from your input alone. Read chapter 3's last paragraph for its parts. Chapter 6 then grades a capstone write-up with a rubric built on the same habits.

excerpts.quote: Record the smallest counterexample, not a large random object that happens to fail.
One mutation at a time makes the resulting evidence causal.
Record the case, prediction, observation, explanation, and one remaining uncertainty for each exercise.

items.title: Why the result is built with Object.fromEntries
items.body:
The key is right: `Object.fromEntries` defines own data properties, so a `__proto__` key stays ordinary data. On a normal object, `result.__proto__ = value` does not create a property called `__proto__`. It calls a special inherited setter that tries to change the object's prototype. For a string value, the worked trace says the assignment is simply ignored, so the key would silently vanish from the output. `Object.fromEntries` *defines* each entry as a plain own property, so `__proto__` is stored like any other key, as the prompt requires.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Direct assignment replaces the prototype with the string": the guide warns against exactly this explanation; for a string it is ignored.
- "It deduplicates keys": the key union is a Set, so keys are already unique.
- "It is faster": speed is not the reason given.

excerpts.quote: That creates an own data property for `__proto__`. Assigning a string to `result.__proto__` on a normal object instead invokes the inherited setter; it does not reliably create the desired data property. For a string value it is ignored, rather than replacing the prototype with a string.
Keys such as __proto__ are ordinary data keys.

items.title: Working the merge trace key by key
items.body:
The key is right: `value = {empty:'', title:'edited'}` and `conflicts = ['note']`. Take the sorted keys one at a time:

- **empty**: base `'x'`, local `''`, remote `''`. Local equals remote, so take `''`. Both editors agreed.
- **note**: base `'absent'`, local missing (deleted), remote `'revised'`. They differ; local differs from base; remote differs from base. Conflict, and local's deletion wins, so `note` is left out of `value` but listed in `conflicts`.
- **title**: base `'draft'`, local `'edited'`, remote `'draft'`. Remote still matches base, so take local's `'edited'`.

Why the others are wrong:
- "empty is 'x' and conflicted": the two editors agree on `''`, so there is no conflict.
- "note is 'revised', no conflicts": both sides changed note differently.
- "Deletions win both keys": `empty` was not deleted by anyone.

excerpts.quote: | empty | x | empty string | empty string | Both editors agree | Keep the empty string |
| note | absent string | M | revised | Both changed differently | Conflict; local deletion wins |
The result has only `empty` and `title`; conflicts contains `note`.

items.title: Why deletion is marked with a Symbol, not a string
items.body:
The key is right: a string marker can collide with a real stored string, and a fresh Symbol cannot. A **sentinel** is a special value that means "nothing here". If the code used the string `'absent'` for "this side deleted the key", a record that genuinely stores `'absent'` would look deleted, and "missing" and "unchanged" could compare equal. The contract allows every string as a value, so no string is safe. `Symbol('missing')` creates a value that is not equal to anything else, so it can never be confused with data.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Empty strings are nullish": they are not; the worked trace says so in as many words.
- "Symbols serialize more compactly": the sentinel never reaches the output; selected sentinels are simply not emitted.
- "Strings compare by locale": `===` compares strings exactly.

excerpts.quote: const missing = Symbol('missing'); const read = (record, key) => (Object.hasOwn(record, key) ? record[key] : missing);
A string fallback still has a real problem: the input domain permits every string, including `'absent'`. Missing and a stored fallback string would compare equal.
The symbol is not needed because empty strings are nullish; they are not.

items.title: What --inventory with --id does
items.body:
The key is right: it prints an error and exits with code 2, because inventory cannot combine with grading. Before doing anything else, `verify.cjs` validates its arguments inside a `try`. One check is `if (inventory && (starters || id !== undefined)) throw Error('Inventory cannot combine with grading')`. The `catch` prints the message and calls `process.exit(2)`. So nothing is listed and nothing is graded. The placement chapter states the same rule.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Silently ignores --inventory": the combination is explicitly rejected.
- "Lists, then grades 3439": validation fails before either step.
- "Grades and appends an inventory section": inventory output is a single console line, never part of the JSON.

excerpts.quote: if(inventory&&(starters||id!==undefined))throw Error('Inventory cannot combine with grading');
catch(e){console.error(e.message);process.exit(2);}
`--inventory` lists the three capstones without grading; it cannot combine with a grading option.
